meta.title: Pool controller · Install
meta.description: Install the pool controller's firmware on an ESP32, from the browser, over USB.

header.title: Pool controller
header.subtitle: Install its firmware from the browser

lede: A filtration controller for a swimming pool, on an ESP32. It drives a variable-speed pump, schedules each day's filtration from the water temperature and the sun, provides freeze protection and counts the fill water. It works on its own; Home Assistant, if you have it, follows and adjusts it.

none.title: No firmware published yet
none.next: The first one comes with the project's next release; this page will then offer it by itself.
none.build: Meanwhile, you can build it yourself from the repository: {make_build} then {make_flash} (see the README).

install.title: Install on a new board

erase.title: Installing erases the board
erase.new: For a new board, or one to start over: everything on it is lost.
erase.never: Never for a controller already in service: it updates itself and keeps its settings (see {updates_link}).

install.hint: Plug the board in over USB, then click: the browser asks which port to use. The board alone is enough to install; the wiring can come later.

dialog.title: In the install window
dialog.note: ESP Web Tools' own, in English
dialog.port: Choose the board's port (often “CP2102”, “CH340” or “USB to UART”), then {connect}.
dialog.port_note: Nothing in the list? A charge-only cable, or the board's USB driver is missing (CP210x or CH34x). Unplug, plug back in, try again.
dialog.install_note: The window warns that everything will be erased: that is intended, every install starts from an empty board.
dialog.wait: The install itself: about two minutes. Keep the page in front, don't unplug.
dialog.wifi: {configure_wifi}: the home network and its password, then {connect}.
dialog.wifi_note: They go through the USB cable (Improv); the controller keeps them only once it is connected. {skip}: it opens its own hotspot instead (see {after_link}).
dialog.visit: {visit_device} opens the controller's page: the rest happens there.
dialog.visit_note: {add_to_home_assistant} can wait: it is the last step of the controller's wizard.

board.name: An ESP32 board
board.note: A development board with an ESP32-WROOM (“ESP32 DevKit”), and its USB port.

relay.name: A 5 V relay module, with 4 channels or more
relay.note: Optocoupled and active-low (the common 8-channel modules work: 4 are used). It closes the pump's inputs.

pump.name: A variable-speed pump
pump.note: With dry-contact control inputs: three speeds and on/off (DI1 to DI4).

probes.name: DS18B20 probes
probes.note: At least one, on the return line to the pool; two more for the equipment pad and outdoors. A 4.7 kΩ resistor between the data line and 3.3 V. Genuine probes: a counterfeit one can block the whole bus.

meter.name: A pulse water meter
meter.note: On the fill inlet, dry contact, 1 pulse per litre: the controller counts the water added.

power.name: A 5 V power supply
power.note: For the board and the relay module.

cable.name: A USB data cable
cable.note: Not a charge-only cable: with one, the board doesn't appear in the list of ports.

computer.name: A computer with Chrome or Edge
computer.note: Windows, macOS or Linux. A phone is then enough to set up the controller.

wiring.probes: DS18B20 probes (1-Wire bus), 4.7 kΩ to 3.3 V
wiring.meter: Water meter; its other wire to GND
wiring.note: Relays on COM/NO: with the board off, they all open and the pump stops. Other pins? They are compiled in: change them in {yaml} and build the firmware yourself. The details: {hardware_link}.

after.title: After the install
after.restart: The controller restarts and joins the Wi-Fi given in the install window.
after.open: Open {address} from a phone or a computer on the same network (or {visit_device}).
after.open_note: If the address doesn't answer: the one your router gives to “{hostname}”.
after.wizard: Its page opens the setup wizard: five steps, a few minutes, and everything stays on the controller.
after.wizard_note: Start right away with the page's password: until there is one, anyone on the network can open it. The Wi-Fi given during the install is already ticked there.
after.ha: Home Assistant, at the last step: add the controller there (Settings › Devices & services › ESPHome; it often discovers it by itself). Home Assistant creates the encryption key and sends it to the controller.
after.ha_note: Without Home Assistant, the controller works too: “I don't use Home Assistant”.

no_wifi.title: No Wi-Fi?
no_wifi.body: Wi-Fi skipped or refused: the controller opens its own hotspot, “{hostname}”, with no Wi-Fi password. Connect a phone to it and open {hotspot_address}: the wizard starts there, with the page's password, then the Wi-Fi.
no_wifi.later: Later, if it loses its network for more than a minute, it opens this same hotspot again.

updates.title: Updates
updates.intro: An installed controller never comes back here.

auto.name: Automatic
auto.note: It looks for a new version every 24 h and installs it (adjustable: on request, 6 h, 24 h, 7 d, in Controller settings › Firmware). Never during an override or a fill: it waits until they end.

request.name: On request
request.note: “Install” on its page (Controller settings › Firmware) or in Home Assistant (Settings › Updates).

kept.name: Settings are kept
kept.note: Password, Wi-Fi, location, probes, Home Assistant key: an update changes none of them.

secrets.name: Built with secrets.yaml (v1.3.x)?
secrets.note: Once, from the repository: {make_migrate}. It keeps all its settings and its Home Assistant key, with no wizard to go through again; after that it updates like the others.

repo.note: The ESPHome firmware, the controller's page, the Home Assistant card. MIT licence. Questions and problems: the repository's issues.
